J2.evidence: Verse 386 «أو مُعْبَرُ الظهرِ يُنْبي عن وَلِيَّتِه» is rendered «whose saddle-cloth shows that…». «يُنْبي» (أنبى/نبا: to repel, make slip off) is read as if it were «يُنبئ» (to inform). The sense is that the thick, unshorn hair (مُعْبَر الظهر) throws off its وليّة (saddle-blanket), as the TR «semerinin altındaki keçeyi atan» correctly has. J1.evidence: Arabic «ولا يُجِيز البصريونَ ذلك إلا في ضرورةٍ»: in grammatical usage ضرورة is the technical term for poetic necessity (licence), so EN «except under poetic necessity» renders the term's meaning, not an addition. Rest of EN checked and faithful.

J2.evidence: The flagged item is a false alarm: in grammatical usage «إلا في ضرورةٍ» is the technical term for poetic licence, so «except under poetic necessity» is accurate. But the EN has other unmarked additions not in the Arabic, notably «it could have meant [many] kinds of each one» for «لاحتمل أن يكون ضروباً من كل واحد», where «[many]» is added. Such additions must go inside «[Translator's note: …]».

J3.evidence: In «ولا يُجِيز البصريونَ ذلك إلا في ضرورةٍ», ضرورة is the grammarians' technical term for poetic licence (الضرورة الشعرية). The Basran rule on dropping the lām/nūn of the oath answer is about verse, so 'except under poetic necessity' is the standard rendering of that term. It translates the written text and adds nothing to it. I checked the rest of the English against the Arabic: «جواب قسم محذوف», «الإلصاق», the reading «بأشياء», the two views on «ونقص» and the five views on «من الأموال» (including Abu al-Baqa and al-Akhfash's زائدة) are all rendered correctly. The source's «لَنَبْلُوَنَّكَ» is kept as written, with a translator's note. Nothing is omitted or mistranslated.
